Article Title: Chinese woman buys around 200 parking spaces in bulk, charges double the original rent and wins legal battle with neighbours
Article Text:
Image Credit: AI Generated

Why did a Chinese woman’s parking space investment spark a legal feud

Wu grabbed an opportunity when others stayed away

What made the parking spaces a source of conflict

The court ruling favoured Wu’s right to own the spaces

The case continues to divide public opinion

A Chinese woman’s decision to buy nearly 200 parking spaces in a residential complex has turned an investment bet into a bitter dispute with her neighbours. Wu spent 14 million yuan, around US$2 million, on the spaces when demand was low, expecting the surrounding area to develop. As the neighbourhood grew and parking became more sought after, she began renting and selling the spaces at higher prices. However, residents who struggled to find affordable parking challenged her ownership in court, sparking a debate over private property rights and access to essential residential facilities.According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Wu bought 196 parking spaces in a residential development in Changsha, Hunan province, in a single transaction. The purchase represented 40% of the project’s total parking inventory.The Star, in its report, also highlighted how the woman’s plan to resell the spaces for profit angered residents and led to legal action. The development’s name was not disclosed in the reports.The dispute began with a decision that initially appeared to be a calculated business move. Instead of purchasing a few spaces for personal use, Wu invested heavily when the property market in the area was struggling.Her neighbours, meanwhile, became concerned when the spaces they needed were increasingly controlled by one owner.The disagreement eventually moved beyond the question of whether Wu could make money from her purchase. It became a conflict over whether a single investor should be able to control such a large share of a residential community’s parking supply.The SCMP reported that the residential project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, the neighbourhood lacked essential amenities, including shops, schools and convenient public transport. Many potential buyers were sceptical about its prospects, and demand for both homes and parking spaces remained weak.Wu took a different view after examining regional development plans issued by local authorities. She believed the area would grow and decided to invest while the developer was facing serious financial difficulties.The developer agreed to sell her the 196 spaces for 14 million yuan, approximately US$2 million. Her decision involved a substantial financial commitment, but it also meant acquiring a large share of the available parking before demand increased.As anticipated, the surrounding area developed, homes in the complex sold more quickly and demand for parking rose. The investment that had looked uncertain during the project’s early days consequently became a source of potential income.She committed her money when others were hesitant, but the resulting ownership concentration later became the central source of friction with residents.According to The Star, Wu installed parking locks to prevent people from using her spaces without permission. She began renting some of them for 500 yuan, around US$75, per month, roughly twice the rental price originally set by the developer in 2018.Residents asked her to reduce the monthly rent to 300 yuan, but she declined. She later listed spaces for sale at around 100,000 yuan, or US$15,000, each, with some asking prices reportedly reaching 80% above their original values.For residents who needed parking, these prices presented a problem. They believed the spaces should be available at the original rates, particularly because parking was an everyday necessity.A government official was sent to mediate between Wu and the residents, but the effort failed to settle the dispute. An undisclosed number of residents subsequently joined forces to challenge the purchase in court.Their argument was that parking spaces formed an important part of the residential community’s infrastructure and should not be monopolised by someone seeking to profit from resale. They asked the court to annul the contract between Wu and the developer.The legal challenge reached a decisive point in February 2024, when a local court in Changsha ruled in Wu’s favour, according to The Star.The court noted that residents had been given the opportunity to purchase parking spaces when the developer initially offered them for sale. They had chosen not to buy them, whereas Wu had committed her money and accepted the financial risks.The court also found that no law restricted the number of parking spaces an individual could own. It therefore considered Wu’s bulk purchase legal and rejected the residents’ attempt to invalidate the original contract.Although Wu’s ownership caused widespread dissatisfaction within the community, the court’s reasoning centred on the original sale and the absence of a legal limit on individual ownership.The SCMP reported that the dispute attracted renewed attention on Chinese social media in late September 2026. Reactions reflected the divide between people who considered Wu a shrewd investor and those who believed parking should primarily serve the needs of residents.Some online users supported her, arguing that the developer had offered the spaces to residents before she bought them. Others questioned whether it was fair for one person to control so much parking while neighbours struggled to find affordable spaces.The court ruling settled the legal challenge to her purchase, but it did not remove the underlying disagreement. For Wu, the spaces represented an investment made with her own money. For her neighbours, they represented access to convenient and affordable parking.
Article Summary: A Chinese woman’s decision to buy nearly 200 parking spaces in a residential complex has turned an investment bet into a bitter dispute with her neighbours. Wu spent 14 million yuan, around US$2 million, on the spaces when demand was low, expecting the surrounding area to develop. As the neighbourhood grew and parking became more sought after, she began renting and selling the spaces at higher prices. Residents who struggled to find affordable parking challenged her ownership in court, sparking a debate over private property rights and access to essential residential facilities. A local court in Changsha ruled in Wu's favour.

Article Title: In 2006, Grand Canyon began a major trout-reduction effort in Bright Angel Creek; after invasive brown and rainbow trout were suppressed, the National Park Service says native fish populations increas
Article Text:
Humpback chub translocation

Native vs non-native

Assessing the results

At least five of the Grand Canyon's eight species of native fish were historically found in Bright Angel Creek. However, these species that are uniquely adapted to the characteristics of the Colorado River and its tributaries have suffered serious declines over the years due to human-caused changes to their habitat. The creek once supported a large number of native fish, including the endangered humpback chub. Humpback chub were first scientifically described from specimens collected in or near Bright Angel Creek. But over the years, it became the main spawning site for non-native brown trout, which are predators of the native population.In 2006, the National Park Service began a multi-year project to reduce the number of non-native brown and rainbow trout to benefit the native fish population. The project was funded by the Bureau of Reclamation and National Park Service, with staff contributions by the University of Missouri and volunteers provided by the Grand Canyon Trust.Alongside efforts to suppress non-native trout, conservationists have also worked to establish and protect humpback chub populations in other parts of the Colorado River system. The endangered fish has been translocated to suitable habitats in the Grand Canyon, including areas where non-native predators pose less of a threat.These efforts aim to improve the species' chances of survival by expanding its distribution and reducing the risks associated with relying on a limited number of spawning and rearing locations.Robust populations of native fish are important indicators of an aquatic ecosystem's overall health. National Park Service Management Policies require that species and natural ecosystems are preserved, and that recovery actions are taken when park resources have been damaged or compromised. A variety of laws, including the Endangered Species Act, require the protection of rare or endemic species.Trout species are not native to the Colorado River and its tributaries in the Grand Canyon. As recently as the 1970s, brown trout were rare in the creek. Brown and rainbow trout were stocked in the Grand Canyon in the first half of the last century before the existence of current environmental regulations and the development of ecological knowledge of aquatic systems. Much of the diet of brown trout in Grand Canyon consists of fish, and they preferentially consume native fish. As their populations increased, there was a corresponding decline in the native fish population.This is where the Bright Angel Creek Trout Reduction Project came in to protect endangered humpback chub and other native fish species in the river and restore and enhance the native fish community. Biologists used two methods for capturing and removing non-native trout in the lower reach of the creek during the winter months: a weir and electro-fishing. The weir captured large trout that live in the Colorado River as they entered Bright Angel Creek to spawn. Electro-fishing allowed fisheries biologists to monitor and assess the fish population of the creek and also remove non-native trout that live in the stream.To date, the Bright Angel Creek Trout Reduction Project has been implemented four separate times during the fall and winter seasons of 2002-2003, 2006-2007, 2010-2011, and 2011-2012. The weir appears to be an efficient way to capture spawning trout. For example, in the 2010-2011 effort, 105 mature brown trout and 107 rainbow trout were captured and removed using the weir.Electro-fishing techniques enable biologists to both monitor native and non-native fish populations and remove non-native fish from the stream. In 2010-2011, biologists removed 594 brown trout and 454 rainbow trout in lower Bright Angel Creek by electro-fishing, estimated to be between 55 and 89% of the trout that were present.The weir has captured larger brown and rainbow trout, up to 25 inches (634 mm) in length, much longer than those captured using electro-fishing equipment. These larger fish carry proportionally more eggs (as much as 20% of their weight) and, because of their size, are more likely to consume native fish. Electro-fishing also allows biologists to collect a wider size range of trout from Bright Angel Creek and allows for biologists to estimate the population size for both the native and non-native fish species.An important goal of the fisheries program is fostering meaningful tribal relations and integrating tribal knowledge and perspectives into its decisions and practices. The program employs a beneficial use policy for all trout removed from the stream, as appropriate, following recommendations received through consultation with traditionally associated tribes. Eleven tribes have cultural connections with the Grand Canyon, including the Pueblo of Zuni, who consider waters connected to Bright Angel Creek and the Colorado River sacred.Following this successful suppression of invasive trout in Bright Angel Creek, native fish populations increased by over 400%, and young flannelmouth suckers were observed rearing in the creek for the first time since brown trout came to dominate the creek
Article Summary: At least five of the Grand Canyon's eight species of native fish were historically found in Bright Angel Creek. These species have suffered serious declines over the years due to human-caused changes to their habitat. In 2006, the National Park Service began a multi-year project to reduce the number of non-native brown and rainbow trout to benefit the native fish population.

Article Title: In 2005, two Ohio brothers bought a flooded quarry for $330,000 and spent 15 years improving it; 21 years later, the village abandoned its bid to seize the 72.5-acre site and now has a $206,000 judgme
Article Text:
After learning about the proposed sale, the Village of Luckey began considering acquiring the property itself. (AI photo)

15 years of improving quarry

What happened at the auction?

Court rejected brothers' claims

Village abandons acquisition but faces bill

What legal bill mean for Luckey

Two brothers in Ohio who bought an abandoned, flooded quarry for $330,000 in 2005 and spent 15 years improving it have been caught in a long legal dispute with the village where the property is located. Steve and Tim Snyder had planned to sell the land in 2021, but the Village of Luckey began proceedings to acquire it through eminent domain, a legal power that allows governments to take private property for public use with compensation.The dispute continued for nearly five years before the village abandoned its attempt to acquire the property in April this year. However, the legal battle has left Luckey facing approximately $206,000 in legal fees, with a judgment lien now recorded against the village.According to a report by The Blade, the amount represents nearly one-third of the village's general fund balance of approximately $640,000 at the end of 2025. The payment has not yet been made because the property owners are challenging the settlement agreement reached by their former lawyer.The case began with a failed property auction in September 2021. The brothers alleged that village officials had discouraged potential buyers from bidding, while Luckey maintained that it wanted the quarry as a possible public water source.The disagreement eventually reached the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, where the brothers' federal constitutional claims were dismissed.Steve and Tim Snyder purchased the inactive quarry and surrounding land in March 2005 through their company, T&S Agriventures LLC. They paid $330,000 for the property, intending to improve it for future development or sale.Over the following 15 years, they worked on the land's topography and grading, cleared vegetation, established electricity and sanitary sewer services, and maintained the quarry lake. Their aim was to make the property suitable for residential or other development.In July 2021, the brothers hired Beth Rose Real Estate and Auctions LLC to market the property. An auction was scheduled for September 18, with a reserve price to prevent the land from selling below an agreed amount.However, after learning about the proposed sale, the Village of Luckey began considering acquiring the property itself. In August 2021, the village council unanimously authorised its attorney to begin the eminent domain process. Officials initially identified a public water supply or park as possible uses, before later specifying water supply alone.Days before the auction, village officials told the brothers that any purchase offer would depend on laboratory results assessing the quarry's water. They also indicated that the eminent domain process could take several years.On the auction day, the village placed temporary 'No parking; signs on nearby public streets. Its representatives attended the event but did not bid.The brothers alleged that the officials' presence discouraged buyers. After bidding closed at $610,000, the property remained unsold because the highest offer was below the reserve price.According to the court documents, the auction company later contacted registered bidders, several of whom said the village's actions had influenced their decision not to bid.The village continued pursuing the land and, in September 2022, offered the brothers $525,000. The dispute subsequently moved into court.The Snyders and their auctioneer filed a federal lawsuit alleging violations of constitutional protections concerning private property, equal treatment and due process.In February 2024, a federal district court dismissed their claims. The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals subsequently upheld that decision.The majority ruled that the village's announcement of its intention to acquire the property did not itself amount to an unconstitutional taking. It noted that the brothers still owned the land and that the $610,000 auction bid demonstrated the property had not lost all economic value.However, Circuit Judge Eric Clay disagreed in a dissenting opinion. He argued that the brothers had presented sufficient allegations of deliberate interference with the auction to allow their takings claim to proceed.The majority also acknowledged concerns about aspects of the village's conduct but concluded that the allegations did not establish a constitutional violation.Luckey continued its attempt to acquire the quarry until April 2026, when the village council formally abandoned the eminent domain proceedings.The decision led to a settlement involving legal fees, with a $206,000 judgment lien recorded against the village in the Wood County Court of Common Pleas.However, the settlement remains disputed. Steve Snyder alleged in court documents that the family's former attorney, Zachary Murry, agreed to the settlement in July without consulting them.The family is seeking to reverse the agreement because it prevents further claims against individual village officials and limits recovery to legal fees rather than additional damages.The village's payment was due on August 15, but Mayor Mike McNulty said officials were waiting for the court to resolve the dispute over the settlement.Luckey, a village of approximately 1,000 residents, ended 2025 with $640,217 in its general fund, according to financial statements cited by The Blade. Its annual revenue was approximately $1.16 million.The potential legal payment is therefore a substantial expense for the village. Nevertheless, McNulty maintained that essential services, including streets, sewer operations and other everyday functions, were not at risk."The village is able to operate functionally," he told The Blade. "We're not going to be able to go and build a swimming pool or something like that. The everyday function of the village, streets, sewer, things like that- the village is fine."
Article Summary: Steve and Tim Snyder bought an abandoned, flooded quarry for $330,000 in 2005 and spent 15 years improving it. They planned to sell the land in 2021, but the Village of Luckey began proceedings to acquire it through eminent domain. The dispute continued for nearly five years before the village abandoned its attempt to acquire the property in April this year. However, the legal battle has left Luckey facing approximately $206,00 in legal fees.

Article Title: A 104-year-old woman finally received her brother's World War II dog tag 83 years after his death; the long-lost identification has now made its way back to the family
Article Text:
The identification tags were found among old military records at Beverly Veterans' Services (Credit: CBS)

How Bernard Parnell died

Discovering the missing tags

How McKay found Stewart

An emotional reunion after 83 years

A 104-year-old woman in Massachusetts has received her brother's military identification tags 83 years after he died in a plane crash during World War II. Dorothy Stewart, who was 21 when her brother Bernard Parnell died in 1943, was reunited with his dog tags at a ceremony held at a YMCA last month.According to CBS Boston, the identification tags were found among old military records at Beverly Veterans' Services. Officials did not know how they had reached the office, but spent several years trying to locate Parnell's surviving family members. Their search eventually led them to Stewart, who was still living in Beverly.For Stewart, the discovery brought back memories of her brother, whose body was never recovered after the aircraft crashed off the Florida coast. Speaking to CBS Boston, she recalled his appearance and popularity when he was young. "First off he was handsome. The girls used to chase him all of the time," she said.The reunion became possible through the efforts of Ken McKay, assistant director of Veterans' Services in Beverly. He had been examining old records when he discovered the tags. A document submitted more than five decades earlier eventually helped him identify Stewart and arrange their return.Bernard Parnell joined the US Navy following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. He subsequently travelled to Florida, where he was training to serve as a radioman aboard an aircraft.His life ended in 1943 when the aircraft developed engine trouble and crashed into the sea off Florida. Stewart remembered what she had been told about the incident, including her brother's actions before the crash. "It had engine trouble and it crashed off the coast of Florida," she said.According to Stewart, Parnell gave a life jacket to the aircraft's pilot, Lieutenant James Digh. The pilot survived the crash, but Parnell did not. "The pilot was the only survivor. My brother's body was never found," Stewart said.With his remains never recovered, the family had no opportunity to bring him home. His military identification tags were also missing for decades, until their discovery among the records maintained by Beverly Veterans' Services.The search began when McKay was going through a collection of historical documents stored in a tote at the veterans' services office. Some of the records dated back to the Spanish-American War.Among the documents were several military identification tags belonging to former service members. Parnell's tags were part of that collection. "This is the fourth or fifth maybe dog tag that we've pulled out of these files," McKay told CBS Boston.McKay could not establish how the tags had originally reached the office. Nevertheless, he began looking for relatives who might still be alive.For approximately four to five years, the tags remained hanging on a frame in his office while he continued his research. According to People magazine, McKay would investigate available records, put the search aside when he reached a dead end and return to it later.As more historical documents became available digitally, he was able to make progress. One record proved particularly useful- an application for a headstone for Bernard Parnell, submitted in 1972. The person who had filed that application was Dorothy Stewart.Finding Stewart's name was an important development, but McKay initially doubted whether she would still be alive. Given the number of years that had passed since the headstone application, he began by searching for her obituary. "Due to her age, I initially just searched for an obituary," he said.Instead, McKay came across a news article about Stewart's achievements in indoor rowing. She had won five consecutive world championships while competing in an age category she described as 95 plus.The rowing article gave McKay a possible way to contact her. He approached the YMCA, explained his position and told staff why he wanted to reach Stewart. "With that, I called the YMCA, and explained who I am. They thought I was a scammer at first," McKay recalled.The YMCA eventually helped establish contact, allowing McKay to arrange the return of the identification tags.On September 29, Stewart attended a ceremony at the YMCA, where her brother's dog tags were formally returned to her. The Beverly Veterans' Council had placed the tags in a frame before presenting them.Receiving the tags brought an emotional response from Stewart, who had lived for more than eight decades without her brother. "I broke down and cried. I just held it after I kissed it. Who would have dreamed after all of this time?" she said.
Article Summary: Dorothy Stewart, 104, was 21 when her brother Bernard Parnell died in 1943. The identification tags were found among old military records at Beverly Veterans' Services. A document submitted more than five decades earlier eventually helped him identify Stewart and arrange their return.

Article Title: Beyonce marked her 45th birthday with a $2 million gift to the Studio Museum in Harlem; it has championed Black artists since 1968 and recently opened a new home
Article Text:
Beyonce's gift and her connection to the museum

A museum founded to champion Black artists

Its artist-in-residence programme supports emerging talent

The museum opened a new home in Harlem

What Beyonce's gift means for the institution

A birthday gift with a cultural connection

Beyonce marked her 45th birthday on September 4, 2026, with a $2 million gift to the Studio Museum in Harlem, supporting an institution dedicated to artists of African descent and the exploration of Black culture through art. Announced by her company, Parkwood Entertainment, the donation reflected her interest in art collecting and her appreciation for the museum's exhibitions, which introduced her to emerging Black artists whose work she admired. The gift came less than a year after the institution opened its purpose-built home in Harlem in November 2025. Founded in 1968, the museum continues to support artists through exhibitions, educational initiatives and professional development programmes.In her birthday announcement, Beyonce highlighted the role art plays in telling stories about the past and present, while noting that it is not always accessible to everyone. She praised the museum for its connection with the community and credited its exhibitions with introducing her to young and emerging Black artists. Thelma Golden, the museum's director and chief curator, thanked the singer for recognising the institution's contribution to Harlem, New York and audiences worldwide.Golden said the gift would help strengthen the museum's work with those communities. Beyonce's interest in the institution connects her personal passion for collecting art with its mission to make the work of artists of African descent more visible.The Studio Museum in Harlem was founded in 1968 by artists, community activists and philanthropists seeking to create greater opportunities for artists of African descent. At a time when their work was underrepresented in many major cultural institutions, the museum established a dedicated space for exhibitions, discussion and the preservation of Black artistic expression. Over the decades, it has developed an internationally recognised programme of exhibitions, public events and educational activities. Its permanent collection contains nearly 9,000 artworks, documenting artistic contributions by artists of African descent from the 19th century to the present.The museum also connects artists with audiences and provides opportunities for professional development, helping emerging and established practitioners develop their work and reach wider audiences.The museum launched its Artist-in-Residence programme in 1969. Since then, it has supported more than 150 artists of African and Afro-Latinx descent, providing resources to develop their practices and establish professional connections. Three artists are selected annually for an 11-month residency. Participants receive studio space, a stipend, research support and professional development opportunities. Their work is presented in a culminating exhibition accompanied by a publication.The 2026 cohort comprised Derriann Pharr, Simonette Quamina and Taylor Simmons. They became the first residents to work in the museum's new building, with their residency running from March through October 2026. The programme reflects the museum's commitment to supporting artists beyond exhibition opportunities by providing the time, resources and institutional support needed to develop their work.On November 15, 2025, the museum opened its new seven-storey building at its longtime location on West 125th Street in Harlem. The 82,000-square-foot facility was designed by Adjaye Associates, with Cooper Robertson serving as executive architect. The building includes exhibition galleries, educational facilities, flexible public spaces and a dedicated artist-in-residence centre. It more than doubled the space available for exhibitions and the residency programme while expanding areas for public engagement.The redevelopment followed a seven-year process and was supported by a fundraising campaign that had raised more than $300 million by the opening. New York State reported a project cost of $160 million and combined state investment of $10.9 million. The new building gives the museum greater capacity to host exhibitions, deliver educational programmes and support artists while maintaining its longstanding presence in Harlem.The $2 million contribution was announced as a gift to the museum, without specifying a particular exhibition, artwork acquisition or programme to receive the entire amount. The institution's wider activities include maintaining its permanent collection, organising exhibitions, supporting artists through residencies and providing educational opportunities. Its expanded facilities offer additional space for these initiatives. Beyonce's statement established a direct connection between her support and the museum's work, particularly its role in introducing her to emerging artists. Her contribution also draws attention to the importance of institutions that provide visibility and professional opportunities for artists whose work has historically been underrepresented.Beyonce's $2 million gift combines her interest in art collecting with support for an institution that has championed artists of African descent for nearly six decades. The timing, following the museum's move into its new Harlem home, places the contribution within a significant period in its history. The donation supports an organisation whose work extends beyond exhibitions to artist development, education and the preservation of Black artistic expression. It also highlights the role that cultural institutions can play in helping emerging artists reach new audiences and build sustainable careers.
Article Summary: Beyonce marked her 45th birthday on September 4, 2026, with a $2 million gift to the Studio Museum in Harlem. The donation reflected her interest in art collecting and her appreciation for the museum's exhibitions. The gift came less than a year after the institution opened its purpose-built home in Harlem in November 2025. Founded in 1968, the museum continues to support artists through exhibitions and educational initiatives.

Article Title: A 1920s Arts and Crafts home in Melbourne's Alphington heads to auction for $3.4 million; the historic home comes with Kookaburra stained-glass windows and distinctive architectural features
Article Text:
Pic credit: Jellis Craig

Pic credit: Jellis Craig

Herald Sun

A historic home with unique character

Pic credit: Jellis Craig

Pic credit: Jellis Craig

Pic credit: Jellis Craig

Inside the Arts and Crafts home

An Arts and Crafts home at 49 Lucerne Crescent, Alphington, is heading to auction with a price guide of $3.1 million to $3.4 million. The two-level home retains its distinctive period features, including Kookaburra stained-glass windows, ornate door surrounds and bespoke details, alongside modern upgrades and a landscaped garden on a 672-square-metre block.The vendors bought the home in 2014 because of its Kookaburra windows. “What I loved about the house was that it felt like the perfect place for a family to spend time together, either in the backyard or the kitchen, and it had a unique style. However, the Kookaburra stained-glass windows were the main reason we bought the house,” the vendor told the. “I love a bit of whimsy, and we actually have a pair of kookaburras who return each year.”Originally built in 1920, the home reflects the Arts and Crafts style of the era. Mass-produced fittings of the Victorian period were in vogue at the time, but the building pushed back against this trend, opting instead for unique, handcrafted features. Those details are easy to spot. The doorways are asymmetrical, with ornate shelves above them. The windows are framed with decorative trim, and the stained glass repeats the theme.Walking through the home, you notice how deliberate those choices look. Nothing feels like a standard catalogue fitting. Even the small details seem to have been drawn by hand.“Its 'Arts and Crafts' character is celebrated through soaring ceilings, shuttered windows and parquetry floors, while state-of-the-art design details enhance the ease of space and flow,” the listing says.According to the listing, the house is a “perfect blend of history and vision”, with its character preserved through the renovations. Its exterior has a quaint, character-filled appeal, while the interiors feature contemporary elements.The two-level home has four bedrooms and four bathrooms, including a downstairs suite and two upstairs bedrooms with en suites and sunny sitting areas. The open-plan kitchen integrates with the living space, while the dining and living area anchors the home. The kitchen has been upgraded with modern appliances, including a Smeg dual-fuel stove and an integrated dishwasher. Outside, there is a garden, a vine-covered pergola, a pool, a spa and a wood-fired pizza oven, making the property ideal for family gatherings and weekends.Between 2017 and 2018, the owners renovated the home. Instead of stripping away its old-world charm, they incorporated it into the modern design. Building designer Ingrid Hornung of Designs for You and local builder Benn Crosbie of Crosbie Constructions oversaw the renovations. The builder recreated some of the original features where possible. The owners also chose handmade pieces to suit the house. These include recycled timber kitchen benches, a custom dining table and a display unit. The dining room light is handmade, and the entranceway chandelier is a 1950s Murano blown-glass piece.Some of the changes were practical. The bedrooms were upgraded with en suites, and walk-in wardrobes were added. There is now a home office, and the kitchen and dining area flow into one open space.For the people who raised their children here, the outside is the real draw. The house sits on a 672-square-metre block with a wide frontage.“Outside is where the house really shines. With picture-book features, the house sits on a big, deep 672 sq m block with a wide frontage. The garden has been lovingly nurtured with plantings of hundreds of bulbs, roses, citrus and stone fruit trees, and a vegetable garden that even the most amateur of gardeners could grow something in,” the vendor told the outlet.There is also an old palm tree in the garden, which is home to parrots that nest every spring.Meanwhile, Jellis Craig’s Paula Beavis is handling the sale. The auction is set for 24 October, and the home is priced between $3.1 million and $3.4 million. Whoever buys the house will also inherit the windows, the handmade lights and, of course, the palm tree. They may also inherit a pair of kookaburras that return every year, whether the new owners ask for them or not!The access is another perk of the home. According to the listing, Alphington Station is an easy stroll away, "offering a direct run into the city, while shopping convenience and cafes nearby take care of everyday needs.""Alphington Park and the Yarra River trails provide plenty of outdoor sanctuaries, and with Alphington Primary School close by and zoning for Kew High School, the location suits family life at every stage," the listing says.
Article Summary: An Arts and Crafts home at 49 Lucerne Crescent, Alphington, is heading to auction. The two-level home retains its distinctive period features, including Kookaburra stained-glass windows, ornate door surrounds and bespoke details. The house sits on a 672-square-metre block with a wide frontage.

Article Title: UK PM says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote, warns Europe faces same threat
Article Text: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union, warning that countries across Europe face the same threat.In excerpts from an episode of “The Rest Is Politics” podcast released on Sunday, Burnham said he asked his advisers after becoming prime minister in July whether Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.“I've had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said.“These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he added.Burnham's remarks come amid warnings from UK intelligence agencies about the growing threat of Russian interference in Britain's democratic institutions. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.Burnham also said he discussed possible links between Russia and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz when the two leaders met in Berlin last week.“You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe,” Burnham said.“There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” he added.In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee found that the British government had failed to fully assess the potential impact of Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts on the EU referendum.
Article Summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the vote. Burnham also said he discussed possible links between Russia and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party.

Article Title: Viola Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island; now she and husband Julius Tennon are donating $1.2 million to help local families
Article Text:
PC: Rhode Island Monthly

A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother

From a childhood in poverty to giving back to her Rhode Island roots

What families will be able to access at the new centre

How the new centre will support thousands of Rhode Island residents

For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood. The award-winning actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a $1.2 million investment in Central Falls, the Rhode Island community where Davis once lived. The money will fund a new family engagement centre named after her mother, Mary Alice Davis, whose influence Davis has spoken about in explaining the project. Planned as a permanent base for local services, the centre will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work.For Davis, naming the facility after her mother gives the project a personal connection. She has described the decision as a way of honouring a woman who continued to believe in people through difficult circumstances. The centre, she said, would carry that spirit forward by supporting individuals and creating opportunities for families.As reported by WJAR, the $1.2 million investment was announced on Monday, 20 July 2026. Rather than funding a single short-term initiative, the donation is intended to establish a lasting community resource in Central Falls, a city closely connected to Davis’s childhood.Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island, an experience that forms an important part of her personal history. She went on to build a career in film, television and theatre, becoming one of the most widely recognised actors of her generation. Her professional achievements have included major industry awards, but her latest investment focuses on a community far removed from the entertainment business.Central Falls was part of the environment in which Davis spent her early years. The new centre offers a way for her and Tennon to direct resources towards residents who may face financial pressures and limited access to services.The couple's contribution is being made through their foundation, which has an existing connection to Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry already serves about 3,000 people each month. The new facility is expected to provide a broader base for that work, alongside services aimed at parents, adults seeking new skills and families looking for guidance.Tennon, who is originally from Austin, Texas, has also expressed his commitment to supporting Rhode Island. Although the state is not his birthplace, he and Davis are directing the investment towards a community that holds particular significance for his wife.The planned facility will bring several services together in one location. These include a parent resource centre, a parent university and adult empowerment programmes, giving parents and other residents access to information and opportunities for learning.Food assistance will remain part of the work. The expanded Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry is expected to build on a service that already reaches thousands of people monthly. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities, educational workshops and community events.For people looking for help with more than one issue, having these services in the same place could make it easier to find the right support. Someone visiting for food assistance, for example, may also be able to access parenting resources or information about employment training.The facility will also serve as the permanent administrative headquarters of the Davis-Tennon Foundation. This gives the organisation a local base from which to coordinate its activities and maintain its work in the area.Angelo Garcia, chair of the foundation, said, "Whether someone comes seeking food, parenting resources, educational support, workforce training, or guidance through a difficult season, our goal is simple: one place where people are welcomed, connected, and empowered.”The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry provides an established starting point for the project. Its reported monthly reach of around 3,000 individuals gives an indication of the demand for food assistance in the community and the role the new centre could play in extending that support.The planned expansion will place the pantry within a wider network of family and adult services. Residents will have access not only to food assistance but also to programmes intended to support education, financial understanding and employment prospects.The centre's effectiveness will depend on how these services are delivered and how well they meet local needs once the facility is operating. The announcement sets out the intended range of programmes, although it does not specify an opening date or provide a detailed timetable for their introduction.By combining food assistance with educational, parenting and employment services, the centre aims to address several practical challenges faced by families in one location.The project also extends the Davis-Tennon Foundation’s existing work in Rhode Island, with the new facility intended to provide a permanent base for its community programmes in Central Falls.
Article Summary: A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother. The actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a new family engagement centre in Central Falls, Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.

Article Title: Taylor Swift donates $1 million to heart charity in honour of her father Scott Swift; US projections warn 6 in 10 adults could have cardiovascular disease by 2050s
Article Text:
PC: Instagram

Taylor Swift’s $1 million gift draws on her family’s experience with heart disease

What the money will support

Why prevention remains a major part of the association’s work

How they support patients and families beyond treatment

Taylor Swift’s latest charitable contribution is tied to a health issue that has affected her own family. The singer has donated $1 million to the American Heart Association in 2025 , directing attention towards cardiovascular disease, its treatment and the work needed to prevent it. The gift honours her father, Scott Swift, whose heart condition she discussed earlier this year. The money is intended to support scientific research, prevention programmes and access to care, according to the organisation. Her contribution also comes as health officials warn that cardiovascular disease is likely to affect a growing share of the American population over the coming decades, placing greater demands on healthcare services.Swift’s contribution recognises her father’s experience with heart disease and supports the American Heart Association’s work across research, public education and medical care. The organisation has not presented the gift as funding for a single project. Instead, it is intended to advance its wider efforts to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease, including work on prevention and improving access to life-saving treatment.As reported by American Heart Association, Nancy Brown, the association’s chief executive, said, “Taylor Swift’s remarkable generosity will create lasting change far beyond its financial value.”She also pointed, “Her family’s experience with cardiovascular disease is all too common, affecting nearly half of American adults. Her commitment to supporting her father will make so many others aware of the need to take their own heart health seriously, strengthen prevention efforts, and improve controllable risk factors—ultimately helping more people live longer, healthier lives.”Swift has previously discussed her family’s experience with cardiovascular disease on the New Heights podcast. Her father’s condition has given the donation a personal connection, although the charity’s work extends well beyond individual cases.The American Heart Association funds scientific research and works to improve how cardiovascular conditions are prevented, identified and treated. Swift’s $1 million gift is intended to advance these efforts, alongside initiatives designed to help more people receive appropriate care.Better understanding of cardiovascular disease can inform clinical practice and contribute to improved treatments. Prevention is another focus, particularly because many of the risk factors associated with heart disease can be identified before a serious event occurs. The association also works to make medical guidance and health information more widely available, with programmes intended to reach communities where access to care may be limited.The organisation's activities include training people in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), publishing medical guidelines, supporting health policy and educating the public about cardiovascular risks. Its work covers more than the treatment of people who have already developed heart disease. It also aims to reduce the likelihood that people will develop serious conditions in the first place.Heart disease and stroke together account for a substantial share of deaths in the United States. The American Heart Association identifies cardiovascular disease as a leading public health challenge, with risk factors ranging from high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol to smoking, physical inactivity and poor nutrition.Some risks are linked to family history, which can make it important for people to understand their relatives’ medical backgrounds. Others can be monitored through routine checks and addressed with medical advice or changes to daily habits. Blood pressure, cholesterol and blood glucose levels are among the measures healthcare professionals use to assess cardiovascular risk.The association advises people to discuss their family history and individual risk factors with a doctor rather than waiting for symptoms to appear. Regular physical activity, a balanced diet, avoiding tobacco and managing stress can also form part of a preventive approach.According to the association, nearly 80% of heart disease cases may be preventable through healthy behaviours. That estimate underlines the emphasis it places on early intervention, although prevention does not remove every risk or guarantee that someone will avoid cardiovascular disease.Swift’s donation supports an organisation that combines research and treatment initiatives with this kind of public guidance. Its aim is to reduce the number of people who develop serious cardiovascular conditions and improve outcomes for those who do.The association has also used the wider conversation around Swift’s donation to encourage people to take cardiovascular health seriously within their own families. Brown referred to the singer’s familiar heart-hand gesture, connecting it with the organisation’s efforts to recognise those affected by heart disease, including relatives and partners who support them.For the charity, the message is closely linked to its public health work: personal experiences can prompt conversations about family history, screening and the steps people can take to understand their own risk.The American Heart Association expects cardiovascular disease to become an even greater burden as the country's population changes and risk factors remain widespread. Its projections indicate that at least six in 10 Americans could have some form of cardiovascular disease within 30 years.
Article Summary: Swift has donated $1 million to the American Heart Association in 2025. The money is intended to support scientific research, prevention programmes and access to care. The gift honours her father, Scott Swift, whose heart condition she discussed earlier this year. Heart disease and stroke together account for a substantial share of deaths in the United States.

Article Title: In 2010, Moby paid $3.925 million for Hollywood’s 1927 Wolf’s Lair, restored the castle-like 3.3-acre estate while preserving its period details, and four years later sold it for $12.4 million
Article Text:
During his ownership, Moby restored the estate while retaining its original architectural character and period details. (Photo: Instagram/Moby)

Wolf’s Lair’s Hollywood history

The estate nearing completion in 1928 (Picture available in public domain)

Moby’s restoration of Wolf’s Lair

The $12.4 million sale

American musician Moby bought a castle-like property in the Hollywood Hills for $3.925 million in 2010 and sold it four years later for $12.4 million. The property, known as Wolf’s Lair, was built in 1927 and stands on 3.3 acres of land above Lake Hollywood in Los Angeles. Its unusual architecture, location and views of some of the city's best-known landmarks made it a distinctive property.Moby, whose real name is Richard Melville Hall, is a DJ, singer and songwriter. According to Los Angeles Times, he purchased the estate from Jay Faires of Lionsgate Entertainment and Debbie Matenopoulos, a former co-host of the television programme The View. The purchase gave him ownership of a property that had been part of the Hollywood Hills for more than eight decades.During his ownership, Moby restored the estate while retaining its original architectural character and period details. The property was already known for its castle-like appearance, with its walls and gates separating it from the surrounding area. Its position above Lake Hollywood also offered views of the Hollywood sign, downtown Los Angeles and the ocean. In November 2014, the Los Angeles Times reported that Moby had sold Wolf’s Lair for $12.4 million.Wolf’s Lair was built in 1927 by L. Milton Wolf, a developer associated with Hollywoodland. The estate takes its name from Wolf and is located in the Hollywood Hills, overlooking Lake Hollywood.Unlike a conventional residential property, Wolf’s Lair was designed with a castle-like appearance. Its enclosed grounds, walls and gates gave it a distinct identity, while its elevated location provided wide views across Los Angeles.The estate occupies approximately 3.3 acres, making the surrounding land an important part of the property. From its position, residents could see the Hollywood sign, the city's downtown area and the ocean.By the time Moby purchased the estate in 2010, the house was already more than 80 years old. Its history and architecture were among the features that distinguished it from other homes in the area. The property had previously belonged to Jay Faires and Debbie Matenopoulos.After buying Wolf’s Lair, Moby undertook restoration work on the property. Rather than changing its established appearance completely, the work was intended to retain the period details that formed part of the estate's identity.Preserving those features was significant because the house dated back to 1927. Its architectural style and castle-like appearance were closely connected to its history, and these remained part of the property following the restoration.Moby owned Wolf’s Lair for approximately four years. During that period, the historic property remained a private residential estate, surrounded by its gated grounds in the Hollywood Hills.Moby later explained that he decided to sell Wolf’s Lair because he wanted a simpler home. In a post published on his official website on December 6, 2014, the musician wrote, "so why did i sell? simplicity." Although he loved the property, he felt that the large estate was more elaborate than he needed. He added, "basically i wanted something simpler than a mountaintop castle."The estate included a main house, a guesthouse designed by architect John Lautner and a pool house apartment. Together, the buildings had eight bedrooms, five-and-a-half bathrooms and approximately 6,500 square feet of living space. The grounds also featured a swimming pool and a terrace with a pergola-covered seating area. The property retained several original architectural features, including coffered ceilings, carved and stencilled beams, turrets and gable windows.
Article Summary: Moby, whose real name is Richard Melville Hall, is a DJ, singer and songwriter. He bought a castle-like property in the Hollywood Hills for $3.925 million in 2010. The property, known as Wolf’s Lair, was built in 1927 and stands on 3.3 acres of land above Lake Hollywood in Los Angeles. Its unusual architecture, location and views of some of the city's best-known landmarks made it a distinctive property.

Article Title: New Yorkers queued for hours to buy discarded subway hardware at an MTA sale where old signs cost $500 to over $1,000, orange seats sold for about $900 and Spike Lee picked up a Penn Station sign
Article Text:
The two-day sale offered old subway signs, seats and MetroCards once used across New York City.

Old subway signs fetch hundreds

Spike Lee buys Penn Station sign

Filmmaker Spike Lee was among the shoppers, purchasing a Penn Station sign

The story behind the MTA sale

Subway seats and MetroCards in demand

New Yorkers waited for hours in south Brooklyn to buy old subway signs, plastic seats and other items removed from the city's transit system at an annual sale organised by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) on Sunday.The two-day sale connected to New York's subway system offered station signs, seats and MetroCards, many of which had once been part of everyday journeys across the city. According to a report by news agency AFP, around 4,000 people attend the event each year.While some signs were priced at more than $1,000, the familiar orange subway seats were sold for around $900 each. Among the shoppers was also filmmaker Spike Lee, who bought a metal sign bearing the name of Penn Station.The sale took place at an open-air market in south Brooklyn, where visitors queued for hours before being allowed inside. To give everyone an opportunity to look through the available items, organisers limited each shopper to 45 minutes. Once their time was over, other visitors could enter and search for what they wanted.Although New York's subway is often criticised for being noisy, dirty and sometimes affected by flooding, many residents still have a strong connection with it.Among those searching for a particular item was 61-year-old Nori Juba, who managed to find a large sign displaying the name of Grand Central station. The sign also carried the numbers of the subway lines he uses every day.Juba acknowledged that the city's subway system has its problems. He described it as "old and creaky and it's outdated," but said those qualities were also part of its appeal."But I think that's what makes it interesting. And this piece of metal is dirty. It smells like a subway station, but there's something about it that makes it real New York, one of a kind in the world," he said.Such items do not come cheaply. A medium-sized subway sign was priced at around $500, while larger signs could cost more than $1,000. The orange plastic seats commonly seen inside New York subway trains were selling for approximately $900 each.Despite the prices, shoppers continued to turn up, hoping to find something associated with their favourite stations or daily journeys.The sale attracted filmmaker and New York resident Spike Lee, who was seen meeting shoppers and posing for photographs.Lee bought a metal sign marked Penn Station, a subway stop associated with Madison Square Garden, where his favourite basketball team, the New York Knicks, plays its home games.Speaking to reporters, Lee recalled using the subway regularly while growing up in New York. Although he no longer takes the train to major basketball games, he said he had always paid for his journeys.He also joked about his record as a passenger, saying, "I never jumped the turnstile either. Let the record state!"The Metropolitan Transportation Authority has sold old subway signs to collectors for years. However, the decision to allow members of the public to browse and purchase the items in person came more recently.Paul Dvoskin, the director responsible for the programme, said the idea developed around five years ago. "Five years ago, an idea was born to hold a garage sale of sorts, and to let people just come in and purchase these items" in person, he explained.The organisers initially called the event a grab-and-go sale, but the response exceeded their expectations. "We called it a grab-and-go back then, and it just ended up being significantly more popular than we ever thought it would be."According to the organisers, the orange plastic subway seats have become particularly popular since they were introduced for sale last year.Another item attracting attention is the MetroCard, the small yellow magnetic card long associated with travel on New York's public transport system. The cards have recently been retired from use and were available at the sale for $6 each.Not everyone arrived with hundreds of dollars to spend. Trinyce and Ijeoma, two women in their twenties, came with a combined budget of $70 and hoped to find something suitable for decorating their apartment.For Ijeoma, the purpose was to bring something connected to the city into her home. "I'd like a piece of New York to represent my living space, like as a representation of me," she said.
Article Summary: Two-day sale connected to New York's subway system offered station signs, seats and MetroCards. Some signs were priced at more than $1,000, while the familiar orange subway seats were sold for around $900 each. Among the shoppers was filmmaker Spike Lee, who bought a metal sign bearing the name of Penn Station.

Article Title: Hurricane Simon pounds Mexico's Pacific coast; Rachel's remnants flood US Southwest
Article Text:
File photo: Damaged homes are seen in Long Beach, Calif., after Tropical Storm Rachel, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.

Rachel triggers deadly flooding in Baja California

Las Vegas records October rainfall high

Hurricane Simon battered Mexico’s Pacific coast on Monday with heavy rain and strong winds, while the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel left communities flooded in the US Southwest. The weather systems caused deaths, damaged homes and roads, and forced evacuations across affected areas.Simon, a Category 2 hurricane, remained offshore as its outer bands lashed communities near Puerto Vallarta. In Guerrero state, the storm uprooted trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and flooded homes, including in the port city of Acapulco, governor Evelyn Salgado said.Reports claim that five people have died due to the hurricane.The US national hurricane center said Simon was expected to remain a hurricane through midweek before making landfall near Sinaloa on Thursday. Rainfall of 5 to 10 inches (12.7 to 25.4 cm) over west-central Mexico in the coming days could trigger life-threatening floods and mudslides.In Puerto Vallarta, workers removed wooden panels from storefronts and businesses reopened as rainfall eased. However, the international airport suspended operations until Tuesday morning.“Personally, I think we should remain on alert because we don’t really know whether it will arrive, move elsewhere or dissipate,” Noelia Carrillo told news agency AP.In Baja California, rescuers searched parts of Ensenada on Monday after floodwaters swept away vehicles and damaged homes. Residents described being caught off guard by the sudden surge of water after heavy rain knocked out electricity.Landslides and overflowing rivers also cut off several communities across the state.The Mexican military used helicopters to rescue 32 people, including 22 foreigners and 13 children, from a ranch in Ensenada. State secretary of security general Laureano Carrillo said some of those rescued were missionaries attending a meeting at the ranch, including Germans and Americans.At least 10 people were reported missing and a young girl was killed in the aftermath of Rachel, Baja California governor Marina del Pilar Ávila said. Around 14,000 federal and state personnel had been deployed to assist residents and respond to the emergency.Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved north into Southern California. It brought unusually large waves that damaged a boardwalk and battered homes in Long Beach, forcing some residents to evacuate.The storm’s remnants also caused flooding in Las Vegas, which recorded 1.08 inches (2.74 cm) of rain by Sunday morning, tying its all-time daily rainfall record for October. The previous record was set in 1947, according to the US national weather service.Videos shared on social media showed floodwaters rushing through a street near the Las Vegas Strip, with casinos and a Ferris wheel visible in the background.Flood advisories were largely lifted by late Monday across Utah, Arizona and other parts of the Southwest.Meanwhile, power restoration continued in the US Southeast after Hurricane Isaias struck the region. At least four deaths have been linked to the storm, which made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, on Friday before moving into Alabama with tropical-force winds.Drier conditions were forecast across parts of the mid-Atlantic and Southeast over the next few days, although temperatures were expected to remain above normal in some areas.
Article Summary: Hurricane Simon battered Mexico's Pacific coast on Monday with heavy rain and strong winds. The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel left communities flooded in the US Southwest. The weather systems caused deaths, damaged homes and roads, and forced evacuations across affected areas.Simon, a Category 2 hurricane, remained offshore as its outer bands lashed communities near Puerto Vallarta.

Article Title: In 2000, Ralph Lauren’s company announced a $5 million gift for a Harlem cancer centre; it opened in 2003 and brought screenings, treatment and practical support to an underserved community
Article Text:
Ralph Lauren (left) with Harold Freeman

Cancer centre opened in 2003

Focused on more than treatment

Further $25 million commitment

American fashion designer Ralph Lauren's company in 2010 announced a $5 million donation to establish a cancer care centre in Harlem, New York, where many residents faced difficulties accessing medical treatment. The centre opened in 2003 through a partnership involving Polo Ralph Lauren Corporation, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and North General Hospital. It was set up to provide cancer screenings, diagnosis, treatment and support to people who had limited access to healthcare.According to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the initiative came after Lauren met Dr Harold Freeman, a cancer surgeon who had spent years working with patients from poor and underserved communities. Freeman had seen many women arrive at hospitals with advanced breast cancer, sometimes after struggling for months to obtain medical help. Their experiences showed him that the problem was not always a lack of willingness to seek treatment, but the difficulties patients faced in reaching it.Some women had been unable to get timely medical attention because of insurance problems, transport difficulties or childcare responsibilities.Others did not know where to seek help. Freeman discussed these problems with Lauren during a meeting arranged through Memorial Sloan Kettering.Recalling their conversation years later, Freeman said Lauren stood up, shook his hand and told him, "I will help you." A few days later, Freeman received a call informing him that Lauren wanted to contribute $5 million towards establishing a cancer centre in Harlem.The Ralph Lauren Center for Cancer Care and Prevention opened in 2003, with Freeman serving as its first medical director.At the time, Lauren explained why he had decided to support the project. "I am inspired by Dr. Freeman's commitment to improving the healthcare and lives of the poor and underserved, not only in Harlem but across the nation," he said.Lauren added that Freeman's work had made him more aware of the community's needs and that he hoped the centre could become a model for similar facilities elsewhere in the United States.The centre initially offered cancer education, screening, diagnostic services, treatment and referrals. Its planned services covered breast, prostate, lung, cervical and colon cancers.An important part of the programme was patient navigation, an approach developed by Freeman to help people move through the healthcare system. Patient navigators assist individuals during their treatment and help them deal with practical problems, including transport, language barriers and difficulties arranging appointments.The centre was designed to make cancer care more accessible and comfortable for residents who might otherwise struggle to receive treatment.According to MSK, the facility offered a welcoming environment, with signs in English and Spanish and staff members who could communicate in multiple languages. The aim was to help patients feel comfortable seeking medical assistance.Its services eventually included screenings for breast, prostate, cervical, skin and lung cancers, alongside community health fairs, educational programmes and nutrition counselling.The approach built on Freeman's earlier work at the Breast Examination Center of Harlem, which provided free breast and cervical cancer screening to women who were uninsured or had inadequate insurance.By the time Lauren's donation was announced, that programme had served more than 125,000 women over approximately two decades.The new centre sought to extend this work by combining screening and diagnosis with treatment and continued patient support.The Ralph Lauren Center faced a major change in 2010 when North General Hospital closed. Memorial Sloan Kettering subsequently became its sole institutional partner, while Lauren continued supporting the facility through the Ralph Lauren Corporate Foundation.In 2019, the centre officially became an ambulatory care centre of MSK, strengthening its connection with the cancer institution.Its partnership with MSK's Immigrant Health and Cancer Disparities Service has helped extend cancer-related services beyond the centr. A Mobile Health Unit provides screenings, education and counselling in New York City neighbourhoods where access to healthcare and transport is limited.Nearly two decades after the centre opened, the Ralph Lauren Corporate Foundation announced another major commitment.In 2022, the foundation pledged $25 million to support the existing Harlem centre and establish four additional centres across the United States.
Article Summary: Ralph Lauren's company in 2010 announced a $5 million donation to establish a cancer care centre in Harlem, New York. The centre opened in 2003 through a partnership involving Polo Ralph Lauren Corporation, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and North General Hospital. It was set up to provide cancer screenings, diagnosis, treatment and support to people who had limited access to healthcare.

Article Title: One dead, several injured in roller coaster incident at Georgia theme park in US
Article Text:
People being evacuated from Six Flags Over Georgia

A man died after being ejected from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, with witnesses describing a horrifying scene in which he struck the ride several times before falling onto the roof of a haunted house attraction below.The incident occurred on the Goliath roller coaster at the amusement park in Cobb County, about 15 miles northwest of Atlanta. Police confirmed one death and said several others were injured, but did not provide details about the injuries or explain what caused the incident.Witnesses told local broadcaster 11Alive that the man appeared to be thrown from his coaster car and struck the ride multiple times as he fell. One passenger said the incident was captured in a souvenir photograph taken during the ride.“He was in our pictures,” the witness said. “He fell and hit the car three different times.” He added that the man’s body struck other riders before landing on the roof of a haunted house attraction.Another couple who were riding the coaster said they saw the man being ejected from his car. “We saw it all,” the man said, while his wife described the moment as they went from enjoying the ride to screaming in shock.A woman told 11Alive that the man had been on the ride with his son, while his wife and daughter watched from the ground.The incident left other riders stranded on an incline and prompted an evacuation of the park. Videos show passengers being helped out of the stationary coaster cars and onto a staircase. The riders were in a car behind the one involved in the fatal incident.The cause of the accident remains unknown. Cobb County Police said detectives from the department’s major crimes unit were investigating.In a statement, Six Flags said it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident” and that park staff and local authorities had responded immediately. The company said it was cooperating fully with investigators and providing support to affected guests and employees.Cobb County board of commissioners chairwoman Lisa Cupid said she could not imagine the horror experienced by park visitors and staff. She added that next of kin had been notified and expressed condolences to the deceased man’s family.“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” Cupid said.
Article Summary: The incident occurred on the Goliath roller coaster at the amusement park in Cobb County, about 15 miles northwest of Atlanta. Police confirmed one death and said several others were injured. Witnesses said the man appeared to be thrown from his coaster car and struck the ride multiple times as he fell.

Article Title: 'Stop oligarchy’: Bernie Sanders turns Musk's India charge on him, slams $366m Trump push
Article Text:
Bernie Sanders targets Musk over $366 million push to keep Republicans in power

Musk’s $276 million push to back Republicans

US Senator Bernie Sanders has criticised Elon Musk for spending $366 million to support Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections, pointing to the tech billionaire’s sharp rise in wealth since backing President Donald Trump’s election campaign.Sanders said Musk had spent $290 million to help elect Trump and had since become $696 billion richer, becoming the world’s first trillionaire. He added that Musk was now spending $366 million to help Republicans retain control of Congress."Elon Musk spent $290 million to elect Trump. It paid off. Since his election, Musk got $696 billion richer & became the world’s 1st trillionaire. But that’s not enough. Now, Musk is spending $366 million to keep Republicans in control of Congress. STOP MUSK. STOP OLIGARCHY," Sanders said in a post on X.This comes as Elon Musk said that Starlink’s entry into India would benefit consumers by offering them more choices, arguing that Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani would remain in business even if competition reduced his profits.In a post on X, Musk criticised what he described as arguments by Ambani’s supporters against Starlink’s entry into the Indian market, calling them “absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole”.“On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor!” Musk wrote.“The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” he added.Musk’s remarks follow an earlier post on Friday in which he addressed Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” and accused him of being the “real boss of India”.“Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India. Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” Musk wrote.The billionaire has also alleged that unnamed business groups are trying to block Starlink’s entry into India to protect their market positions. The government has rejected these allegations, maintaining that the delay is due to pending regulatory and security requirements.According to a report by The New York Times on Monday, Musk has spent $276 million since July alone, including $158 million through a super PAC focused on Republican Senate candidates. The report identified him as the largest single donor this year.Musk, considered a close ally of Trump, served as a special government adviser to the White House last year. His political action committee, America PAC, has confirmed the spending figures.Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, defended the expenditure, saying it was necessary to prevent Democrats from taking control of Congress in the midterm elections.“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told The New York Times.The spending comes as Republican candidates contend with Trump’s low approval ratings and growing concerns among voters over the cost of living. Democrats are seeking to capitalise on dissatisfaction with the president’s tenure and regain control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Article Summary: US Senator Bernie Sanders has criticised Elon Musk for spending $366 million to support Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. Sanders said Musk had spent $290 million to help elect Trump and had since become $696 billion richer, becoming the world’s first trillionaire.

Article Title: Architect Andrew Batey designed this 1972 glass house for a photographer; the Berkeley Hills home with a former darkroom is listed for $1.088 million
Article Text:
Image: Left/Harry Bowles (Credit: Manitoba Historical Society Archives)/Right/Matt Harper/NorCalHomeTours

Andrew Batey designed the Berkeley glass house for photographer Henry Bowles

The two-storey glass façade brings Berkeley’s woodland into the home

"The Photographer's House,” at 141 Fairlawn Dr. in Berkeley (Image: Matt Harper/NorCalHomeTours)

A floating staircase, loft bedroom and skylit bathroom shape the interior

The former darkroom adds a creative legacy to the $1.088 million listing

A glass house nestled among the trees of California’s Berkeley Hills is attracting attention for its unusual architecture and creative history. Designed in 1972 by architect Andrew Batey for architectural photographer Henry Bowles, the residence was conceived to connect its interiors with the surrounding woodland. The two-bedroom property combines glass, steel and redwood in a design that makes natural light and the landscape central to its character. Now listed for $1.088 million, the home is being offered after more than two decades under its current owner. Its former photographic darkroom, double-height living room and distinctive glass façade add to its appeal.The story of the Photographer’s House began in 1972, when architectural photographer Henry Bowles commissioned a residence that reflected his appreciation for design and natural light. According to SFGATE, Bowles had trained under renowned Western photographer Morley Baer before establishing his own professional reputation. Architect Andrew Batey, who was 28 when he undertook the project, designed the house using glass, steel and redwood. The commission brought together Bowles’s interest in architectural photography and Batey’s developing modernist approach. The residence is identified as one of Batey’s early commissions, predating his subsequent work with architect Mark Mack at the firm Batey and Mack.The house therefore offers a glimpse into the architect’s early career while preserving the creative vision behind its original commission.The property’s defining feature is its expansive glass façade, which creates a visual connection between the interior and the wooded hillside outside. According to the New York Post, the 1,625-square-foot house combines glass, steel and redwood to create a distinctive modernist residence. Its double-height living room gives the relatively compact home a sense of openness, while sliding glass doors lead towards a spacious deck. Realtor also highlighted the two-storey glass wall as a defining feature of the property, helping explain its appeal to readers interested in distinctive homes. Rather than placing conventional walls between residents and the landscape, the design allows trees and daylight to become part of the visual experience.
