NEW DELHI: India on Sunday accused Pakistan of using allegations about the treatment of religious minorities in India to divert attention from its own record on minority rights, judicial independence and press freedom.Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly's Sixth Committee during discussions on the rule of law at national and international levels, Mythili R, a counsellor at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, accused Islamabad of preaching legal accountability abroad while undermining it at home.She described Pakistan as a country where "the army is the rule and the law", alleging that judicial independence had been weakened, civilians were being tried in military courts and political opposition was being suppressed."At the UN, Pakistan lectures others on the rule of law. Yet at home, the Army is the rule, and the Army is the law. Judicial independence undermined, civilians tried in military courts, political opposition suppressed," she said, according to a statement shared by India's Permanent Mission to the UN on X.Mythili also challenged Pakistan's claims on minority rights, pointing to what she described as a steady decline in the proportion of minorities in the country's population since its creation.She questioned press freedom in Pakistan, referring to the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines issued by its Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Under the guidelines, foreign media outlets must obtain a "No-Objection Certificate" to report freely outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi.The Indian diplomat accused Pakistan of repeatedly failing to uphold the rule of law and said its focus on India was misplaced."The rule of law bestows an obligation upon those in positions of power to do good for those they govern. However, in the case of Pakistan, unfortunately, this promise is broken again and again. It is not India that has an obsession with Pakistan but the other way round," she said.The exchange also brought the two countries' sharply contrasting positions on cross-border terrorism into focus. Mythili defended India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in Pahalgam last year, which killed 26 people, describing Operation Sindoor as measured and proportionate.She urged Pakistan to stop repeating what she called baseless allegations against India, arguing that doing so would not shield its representatives from accountability for promises made to their own people."Reading and re-reading the same laundry list of false allegations against my country will not absolve Pakistani representatives of the promises that they have made to their people and which they have no intention to keep," she said.Taking a swipe at Pakistan's claims about the outcome of the military confrontation, she added, "As far as the result of the same is concerned, if bombed airfields and destroyed hangars are victory, they are welcome to enjoy it," she said.The latest exchange followed India's response on Saturday to Pakistan's remarks at the UN General Assembly's First Committee, where discussions included disarmament and international security.First Secretary Anmol Sher Singh Bedi said India's military posture was defensive and guided by its own security requirements, rather than directed against any particular country. He defended India's response to the Pahalgam attack as "measured, targeted, and non-escalatory" and an exercise of its right to self-defence.Bedi laid out India's position on terrorism and the risk of nuclear escalation, stating, "First: Any terrorist attack against India will receive a fitting response; Second: India will not bow to nuclear blackmail; Third: India will make no distinction between those who sponsor terrorism and those who mastermind it."He argued that states could not escape responsibility for supporting militant groups by acting through non-state actors, adding that such actions did not diminish India's right to defend itself."Escalation concerns are best judged by conduct, over rhetoric. Nuclear weapons must not be a routine instrument of statecraft. Relying on a nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of sub-conventional activity raises escalation risk, not restraint," he said.Bedi also criticised what he described as a recurring pattern in regional crises, involving provocation, denial of responsibility and calls for restraint after retaliation.He said, "where those in power are neither elected by nor accountable to the people, crisis becomes an instrument of power and instability becomes useful."Reaffirming India's stated commitment to peace, Bedi said the country did not seek conflict but would respond to threats. He concluded, "without accountability for reckless actions, peace merely becomes a pause between crises."
Article Summary: Mythili R, a counsellor at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, accused Islamabad of preaching legal accountability abroad while undermining it at home. She described Pakistan as a country where "the army is the rule and the law" Mythili defended India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in Pahalgam last year.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Chilling videos show bridges swept away, homes destroyed
Article Text:
Dramatic videos show scale of destruction after flash floods hit Nepal

A short while ago: A devastating flash flood has swept away Salleri Bazaar (Market) and caused severe destruction in Jagat Bazaar along the Budhi Gandaki River, Gorkha District, Nepal.(Video provided by Umesh.) https://t.co/aK74PD0S5t— Weather Monitor (@WeatherMonitors) October 11, 2026

Homes, bridges swept away as floodwaters surge

Army, helicopters deployed for rescue operations

Bihar monitors possible impact as flood wave moves downstream

Dramatic videos from Nepal show the scale of destruction caused by a flash flood along the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha district, with entire sections of settlements swept away, bridges destroyed and homes reduced to debris.Visuals from the affected region show floodwaters tearing through Salleri Bazaar, causing severe damage in Jagat Bazaar and sweeping away bridges and other infrastructure.Other footage shows homes, buildings and bridges being carried away by the powerful, debris-laden waters.More than 80 people, including nine foreign nationals, have been rescued, while five people remain missing, according to news agency PTI.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said the missing include two women. The full extent of the damage remains unclear.The flooding has devastated settlements in the northern part of Gorkha district, including Salleri, Jagat, Dovan and Ghattekhola. Preliminary reports had suggested that around 35 houses were swept away in the affected areas.The NDRRMA said 45 houses were completely destroyed and another 27 suffered partial damage.The floods and landslides also damaged two suspension bridges, two motorable bridges, three hydropower projects and 34 cattle sheds, while three vehicles were swept away.The flood followed a landslide that blocked the Budhi Gandaki River between Lokpa and Chhumling on Sunday morning, according to news agency ANI.The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), citing preliminary accounts from Nepal's authorities, said the flooding may have been triggered by the failure of a temporary blockage created by a landslide near Chumchet in Gorkha district.The floodwaters swept away bridges connecting several settlements, including the bridge linking Nyakchet and Philim Bazaar. Damage also affected the bridge connecting Arughat in Gorkha to Dhading, the suspension bridge linking Nyakchetat and Sirdibas, the Machhikhola-Kerauja footbridge and the bridge at Sotima.The disaster also damaged energy infrastructure. Floodwaters swept away the main camp area and equipment at the Budhi Gandaki hydropower project under construction in Salleri.The flood damaged two telephone towers and 50 electricity poles, while 20 to 22 houses in lower Machhakhola were at immediate risk.Authorities have yet to establish the precise cause of the sudden surge. Residents cited by PTI said the river's flow appeared to stop and resume, while some reported that it had not rained when the flooding began.Nepal has mobilised security personnel and helicopters to evacuate residents and provide relief in the affected region.Prime Minister Balendra Shah said a Nepali Army contingent had been deployed by air and land for search and rescue operations. A rapid response team from Kathmandu was also airlifted to the area.The rescue count increased as operations continued. The Nepal Army initially reported evacuating six people to safer locations. According to a later update, 36 people, including one foreign national, had been rescued in the army's response.By the time of reporting, 82 individuals, including nine foreign nationals, had been rescued using four helicopters.More than 700 security personnel had been mobilised, including 171 Nepal Army soldiers.NDRRMA had mobilised 437 personnel from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force.Authorities have also sent tents, blankets, mattresses, sleeping bags and kitchen sets to affected areas.Home minister Sudan Gurung urged people living along the Budhi Gandaki River to move to safer areas and remain alert as the river's flow continued to fluctuate. Police, the Armed Police Force and local authorities have been mobilised for rescue, relief and evacuation efforts.The NDRRMA has also advised residents along the riverbanks to move away from riverbeds, avoid damaged bridges and roads, and follow instructions from local security agencies.Authorities have dispatched a specialised team, including geologists, and drones to investigate the landslide. Officials are also examining the feasibility of installing emergency Bailey bridges.Tourists travelling for the Manaslu trek have also been stranded after floodwaters washed away a footpath and a bridge. The Manaslu Conservation Area Project said the tourists were safe at their accommodation.The flood has also prompted monitoring in neighbouring Bihar. Deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Choudhary said no significant impact was expected at the Valmikinagar barrage in West Champaran district.Choudhary said the flood wave had crossed Devghat, around 80 km upstream of the barrage. The discharge was expected to rise by around 15,000 cusecs before returning to normal levels, he said, adding that the situation was being closely monitored and precautionary measures had been taken.Officials had initially estimated that the flood wave could raise the barrage's discharge by around 25,000 cusecs from approximately 50,000 cusecs to 75,000 cusecs, but Choudhary said this would remain within normal limits.The disaster comes around a month and a half after the devastating Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river floods on August 26. Nepal is still recovering from that disaster, which left more than 1,400 people dead and 5,285 missing.
Article Summary: Dramatic videos from Nepal show the scale of destruction caused by a flash flood along the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha district. More than 80 people, including nine foreign nationals, have been rescued, while five people remain missing. Floodwaters swept away bridges connecting several settlements, including the bridge linking Nyakchet and Philim Bazaar.
